summary: Registers media types for ECMAScript and JavaScript and sets conformance requirements for implementations, aligned with current usage. It obsoletes RFC 4329. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This says what label a JavaScript file should carry when it travels over the web.

questions: what is the javascript mime type
subtitle: Registers text/javascript as the media type for JavaScript and ECMAScript and retires the older names.

tldr.problem: The earlier registrations in RFC 4329 steered people towards application/* types, but the industry widely used text/javascript anyway, and the rules for modules and character encoding were missing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC makes text/javascript the one common media type, marks the other names as obsolete aliases, says how to pick a character encoding and registers the .mjs extension for modules.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4329 and aligns the registrations with common usage. The IESG note says this is not an IETF endorsement of the media types chosen.

today: RFC 9239 is an Informational RFC published in May 2022 that obsoletes RFC 4329, and no later RFC obsoletes it. It remains the document that registers text/javascript with IANA.

sections.title: Purpose and Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 9239 describes media types for the JavaScript and ECMAScript programming languages and replaces the registrations in RFC 4329. It defines equivalent processing requirements for the various script media types. The most widely supported one is text/javascript, and all others are considered historical and obsolete aliases.

The types apply to scripts written in ECMA-262. Later editions of that standard are not addressed directly, but implementations are expected to behave as if the types applied to them. The document does not define how fragment identifiers are resolved for these types.

An IESG Note says the relationship between Ecma International's TC39 and these media types was developed outside the IETF and does not follow BCP 13. The IETF documents it and updates the IANA registrations, but does not endorse the media types chosen.
sections.eli5: There used to be many labels for the same kind of file. This document says one label is the real one and the rest are old nicknames.

sections.title: Scripts and Modules
sections.content:
ECMA-262 defines two top-level goal symbols, Script and Module, starting with its 6th Edition. Script code runs in the global scope, and Module is the built-in module system. For any given source text there are two possible interpretations.

The RFC says it is not possible to tell from content or media type alone which goal applies, and TC39 considers media types outside its scope. Environments therefore use out-of-band information, and some have adopted the file extension .mjs to signal a module.
sections.eli5: A JavaScript file can be one of two kinds, and the label alone cannot say which. So some people mark the module kind with a special file ending.

sections.title: Character Encoding Rules
sections.content:
The types allow an optional charset parameter. It is optional rather than required, despite the BCP 13 recommendation for text types, in order to match common practice. Implementations that support binary source text MUST support UTF-8. Module sources MUST be encoded as UTF-8, and Script sources SHOULD be, with other encodings discouraged.

To pick an encoding, implementations apply this order until one is determined.

  1. If the text is not already known to be a Module and starts with a Unicode signature, the signature decides.
  2. Otherwise, a valid and supported charset value decides.
  3. Otherwise, UTF-8 is assumed.

If UTF-8 is determined by some means other than the signature and the text starts with EF BB BF, those octets are ignored when decoding. For text in an unsupported or invalid encoding, the RFC says implementations can consider the resource unsupported, and can substitute U+FFFD for invalid sequences or stop processing.
sections.eli5: Before reading a note you need to know which alphabet it is written in. First look for a secret sign at the start, then the label, and if there is nothing, assume the usual one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that uncontrolled execution of scripts can be exceedingly dangerous. Implementations that execute scripts MUST consider their threat models and MUST ensure that untrusted content is not executed in an unprotected environment. They MUST also protect against denial of service from features such as eval() that can run dynamically generated source text.

Other points include the risk that an imported module can expose information such as an IP address to the host it is fetched from, code injection when external input reaches eval(), and timing side-channel attacks made possible by SharedArrayBuffer objects. Implementations MUST take steps to avoid confusion about the origin of messages shown to the user, and source text is expected to be in Unicode Normalization Form C.
sections.eli5: Running a script means following instructions from a stranger, so a program must only do that inside a safe room.

sections.title: The IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The registrations fall into two groups: the sole common type, text/javascript, and a list of obsolete types, including application/javascript, application/ecmascript and text/ecmascript. The published specification for all of them now points to ECMA-262, and the intended usage of text/javascript moves from OBSOLETE to COMMON.

The registration for text/javascript lists the file extensions .js and .mjs, and says that .mjs files are parsed using the Module grammar. IANA added the note OBSOLETED in favor of text/javascript to the other registrations. Four legacy types with an x- prefix are kept only for backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: The official list now shows one main label for JavaScript and puts the old labels in a box marked old.
